reason: Chest pain is a listed sign of cardiac distress, and the ambulance report documents chest pain; transport to a hospital is a presumed appropriate destination.

Both PT and OT were provided, measurable improvement was achieved, and she came from a SNF after the acute stay; intensity is asserted and consistent with the combined therapy times, so two agents support coverage.
A caregiver already gave oral meds and insulin, and the beneficiaries were stable at discharge, so a skilled nursing need and skilled observation are not shown.
Coumadin doses were adjusted twice with INR out of range, so prothrombin monitoring and skilled observation were reasonable and necessary under a plan of care specifying services and frequency.
Transport was for nausea and she was treated and released; no showing that other transport was contraindicated, so medical necessity is not established.
The appellant concedes ground transport was reasonable, the patient was stable, and a closer equipped facility existed, so air ambulance is not supported.
A neurosurgeon recommended transfer to the Neuro ICU for a hemorrhagic stroke, which fits a covered inter-facility transfer; nothing in the record shows a nearer appropriate facility.
The destination is not shown to be a SNF or hospital, and the run sheet says he could stand and walk, undercutting the contraindication of other transport.
Therapy intensity and physician face-to-face visits are not shown in the record, so the IRF requirements are not established despite functional gains.
The inpatient status was recorded as made in error and reverted to observation; the discharge summary says overnight observation, so inpatient admission requirements are not met.
The destination was recorded as a clinic, and ambulance service to a physician-directed clinic is not covered; no showing it was a hospital or SNF.
Re-certification documents inability to leave home without taxing effort, and the infrequent absences for adult day care and doctor visits do not disqualify homebound status.
The beneficiary was admitted as an inpatient after observation with chest pain, new T-wave inversion, extensive cardiac history and catheterization; the stay is consistent with inpatient admission.
The transferring hospital lacked cardiology, but it is not shown that Wichita was the nearest appropriate hospital or that ground transport would endanger health.
Physician-ordered dysphagia therapy by a speech-language pathologist was skilled, documented progress, and coverage does not depend solely on improvement potential.
Skilled observation requires a reasonable potential for change, and care continued about sixteen months with no instability described; need is not supported.
Homebound status is not established: she attends day care four days a week, travels independently, and moves independently, and day care licensure is not shown.
Nurse visits only to pour a mediplanner are not skilled, aide hours exceed the 28-hour weekly limit, and no skilled observation rationale is documented.
The inpatient stay was for a complex hernia repair with significant pulmonary disease, and nothing in the passages shows the services were non-covered.
Nurses provided documented pressure ulcer and wound care and caregiver teaching, with diabetes as a factor affecting healing, which is skilled nursing.
Family gave medications and monitored glucose, services family can safely perform are not covered, and documentation of skilled need is vague.
Physician-ordered gait training and range-of-motion PT improved her fall-risk score from 7/28 to 18/28, with a plan of care specifying type and frequency.
